title: A Former Ship Captain Ran a Cyber Slavery Pipeline From India to Cambodia. Police Say Hundreds May Have Been Trapped.
excerpt: Nagesh Kumar, alias Captain Chauhan, charged victims Rs 3.5 lakh each for fake overseas jobs, then smuggled them into Chinese-run scam centres where they were forced to defraud fellow Indians.
body:
The arrest, when it came, was almost anticlimactic. Nagesh Kumar — a former merchant navy captain who goes by the alias Captain Chauhan — was picked up in Chandigarh after six months on the run, brought to Agra on a transit remand, and is expected to be produced before a court this week. The charges are anything but routine: police allege he masterminded an international trafficking network that lured Indian youths to Cambodia and Laos with promises of dollar-salary jobs, then handed them over to Chinese-run cyber scam operations.

## The Pipeline

The operation, according to Agra Cyber Crime Police, worked with industrial efficiency. Kumar and his network of agents — spread across multiple Indian states — targeted young men from economically vulnerable backgrounds with social media advertisements promising lucrative overseas employment. Victims were charged up to ₹3.5 lakh each for the "placement process." They were initially flown to Bangkok on legitimate travel documents, then smuggled across borders into Cambodia and Laos through illegal routes.

Once there, the job descriptions changed. Victims were confined in compounds run by Chinese cyber fraud companies and forced to work as scam operators — making calls to Indian citizens to execute digital arrest scams, online lottery frauds, investment cons, fake customer-care operations, and banking fraud. Indian nationals were specifically chosen because they could communicate fluently in Hindi and other Indian languages, making it easier to gain victims' trust.

Those who refused to participate allegedly faced physical assault, mental harassment, and confinement. Their passports and travel documents were confiscated. In some cases, families back in India were pressured to send additional money — a second extraction from people who had already been defrauded.

## The Scale

Investigators believe the network operated for approximately three years and that hundreds of Indian youths may have been trafficked through it. The operation came to light after a few victims managed to escape and return to India, where they approached the police with detailed accounts of their ordeal. Three other members of the network were arrested earlier; their interrogation led police to Kumar, who was eventually tracked down through technical surveillance and intelligence inputs.

The Agra Cyber Crime Police have recovered Kumar's mobile phone, which contained WhatsApp chats with foreign contacts and digital evidence linked to Chinese cyber companies. Forensic analysis of the chats, bank accounts, and travel records is ongoing.

## A Growing Crisis

Kumar's arrest is a data point in a much larger crisis. India has emerged as both a source country for cyber slavery victims and a primary target market for the scams those victims are forced to run. The Ministry of External Affairs has acknowledged rescuing at least 130 workers from Southeast Asian scam compounds. Independent estimates suggest the true number of trapped Indians runs into the thousands.

The scam centres themselves are sophisticated operations. They are typically housed in large compounds — some resembling office parks — in Cambodia, Myanmar, and Laos. Workers operate in shifts, running multiple fraud campaigns simultaneously. The operations generate billions of dollars annually, with proceeds laundered through cryptocurrency and shell companies across multiple jurisdictions.

Prof. Triveni Singh, a former IPS officer and cyber crime expert, warned that international cyber gangs are increasingly using social engineering and fake overseas job offers to trap Indian youths. "People should thoroughly verify recruitment agencies and foreign job offers before making payments or sharing personal documents," he said. "Such fraud networks are becoming more organised and transnational in nature."

## What NRIs Should Know

For the Indian diaspora, this story carries a particular urgency. Many of the "digital arrest" scams that trapped victims are forced to run specifically target NRIs — exploiting their distance from Indian institutions and their unfamiliarity with current procedures. Common tactics include callers posing as customs officials claiming a package with illegal contents was intercepted, or as police officers alleging a family member's involvement in a crime.

The advice from law enforcement is straightforward but worth repeating: no Indian government agency conducts arrests or legal proceedings over phone or video call. No legitimate recruitment agency charges ₹3.5 lakh upfront for overseas placement. And if a family member in India mentions a sudden overseas job opportunity that sounds too good to be true, it almost certainly is.

Kumar's journey — from merchant navy captain to alleged trafficking mastermind — is a reminder that cyber crime in 2026 is not the work of lone hackers. It is an industry, with supply chains, human resources, and operational infrastructure that spans continents. The victims at the bottom of that supply chain are, disproportionately, young Indians who were promised a future and delivered into servitude.
author: Diaspora Desk
